title: Minor Head Injury in Children: Observation and CT Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Emergency, urgent care and primary health centre doctors and nurses in Saudi Arabia assessing a child under 16 years with a head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13 to 15: decide who needs a computed tomography (CT) head scan within 1 hour, who needs at least 4 hours of observation, who can go home, and what to tell the family. Uses NICE NG232 (2023), the PECARN rule study and Saudi paediatric data. Not for children with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12 or less, penetrating injury or major trauma (follow the paediatric trauma pathway).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Health Council guideline for paediatric minor head injury was found; the thresholds are NICE NG232 (2023) and the Saudi data are descriptive only.
NICE NG232 is a United Kingdom guideline; local availability of 24-hour computed tomography, paediatric radiology reporting and paediatric observation units in each Saudi region was not checked.

The PECARN rule study abstract was read, not the full paper: the definition of severe injury mechanism in the PECARN rule and the exact decision between observation and scanning are not written here, and NICE criteria are used for the scan decision.

NICE says safeguarding concerns and suspected non-accidental injury need a scan within 1 hour; the Saudi child protection referral route (for example the national child protection reporting line) was not verified and is not written.

The paracetamol (acetaminophen) dose is taken from a United States over-the-counter children's label that gives doses by weight band for ages 2 to 11 years and says to ask a doctor for those under 2 years; a per-kilogram dose for infants was not found in the sources and is for the treating clinician to set.
Tranexamic acid for a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12 or less (NICE Recommendation 1.3.17) is outside this topic's Glasgow Coma Scale range and is not written as a regimen.
Rates of delayed presentation, post-concussion symptoms and school return advice in Saudi Arabia were not found; the return-to-school advice is from NICE only.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web, article and label text; spot-check each figure and dose against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: A child's skull is thinner and softer and the brain is less myelinated, so the same force can cause more injury than in an adult (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Introduction). Primary injury is mechanical damage at impact; secondary injury develops hours to days later (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Introduction). Most serious injuries are rare after a minor injury: in 42,412 children with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14 to 15, clinically important traumatic brain injury occurred in 0.9% and neurosurgery in 0.1% (PECARN rule study, Section Findings). Computed tomography carries a radiation risk of cancer in children, so scanning is reserved for children at higher risk (PECARN rule study, Section Background). Falls cause most injuries in babies and children under 6 years, and road traffic collisions are the most common cause in older children in Saudi Arabia (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Results).

symptoms: Headache, vomiting, drowsiness or irritability after the injury; ask about each, because they are scan or observation triggers (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).
Loss of consciousness or amnesia: it is not possible to assess amnesia in preverbal children and unlikely in those under 5 (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.2.3).
Altered behaviour, being easily distracted or not acting like themselves, especially in babies and children under 5 (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.2.3).
A seizure since the injury (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
physicalSigns: Glasgow Coma Scale below 14 at first assessment, or below 15 for babies under 1 year using the paediatric scale (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Glasgow Coma Scale below 15 two hours after the injury (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture, or tense fontanelle (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Basal skull fracture signs: blood behind the eardrum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid from the ear or nose, Battle's sign (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Focal neurological deficit; in a baby under 1 year a bruise, swelling or laceration over 5 cm on the head (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
redFlags: Suspicion of non-accidental injury: scan within 1 hour and start safeguarding (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit, Glasgow Coma Scale below 14 (below 15 if under 1 year), or signs of skull fracture: scan within 1 hour (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).

More than one of: loss of consciousness over 5 minutes, abnormal drowsiness, 3 or more vomits, dangerous mechanism, amnesia over 5 minutes, bleeding or clotting disorder: scan within 1 hour (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).
During observation: Glasgow Coma Scale below 15, further vomiting or further abnormal drowsiness: scan within 1 hour (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.12).
Do not send a child for a head scan by direct access from the community (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.3.19).
precipitants: Falls in babies and young children, the most frequent mechanism under 6 years (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Results).
Road traffic collisions in children aged over 6 to 14 years, 42.7% of injuries in that group (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Results).
Male sex, 67.9% of injured children in the Jeddah series (Jeddah children's head injury study, Section Results).
Bleeding or clotting disorder (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).
Dangerous mechanism: high-speed road traffic collision as pedestrian, cyclist or occupant, fall over 3 m, high-speed projectile (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Brief symptoms, normal Glasgow Coma Scale, and no scan criteria met; needs home supervision and return advice (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.10.9).
Soft tissue injury; a swelling over 5 cm in a baby under 1 year needs a scan (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Drowsiness, vomiting, seizure, focal deficit or basal skull fracture signs (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
History inconsistent with the injury, unexplained bruising, or delayed presentation; safeguarding concern requires a scan within 1 hour (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Use clinical judgement about the cause of vomiting in children 12 years or under (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.2.4).

ruleIn.testName: Computed tomography head scan within 1 hour for a single high-risk factor
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Detect skull fracture and intracranial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Haemorrhage, contusion, fracture or oedema on the report
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Triggered by non-accidental injury, seizure, low Glasgow Coma Scale, skull fracture signs, focal deficit or large head swelling in a baby (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
ruleIn.normalValue: No acute intracranial abnormality reported by the radiologist

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Detect injury in children with two or more moderate-risk features
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Haemorrhage, contusion or fracture on the report
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Applies when more than 1 of the six listed factors is present (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).
ruleIn.normalValue: No acute intracranial abnormality reported by the radiologist

ruleIn.testName: Computed tomography head scan on deterioration during observation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: New abnormality when Glasgow Coma Scale falls, vomiting recurs or drowsiness recurs
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Observed children with only one factor are scanned within 1 hour if any of these appear (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.12).
ruleIn.normalValue: No acute intracranial abnormality reported by the radiologist

ruleOut.testName: Normal computed tomography head scan with Glasgow Coma Scale of 15
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Support discharge when the child has recovered
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No abnormality on the provisional written report available within 1 hour
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A provisional written radiology report should be available within 1 hour of the scan (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.14).
ruleOut.normalValue: Normal scan with Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 and normal consciousness for age

ruleOut.testName: Repeat computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging head scan
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Look for injury when the Glasgow Coma Scale is not 15 after 24 hours despite a normal scan
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Consider a further scan and discuss with radiology (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.16).
ruleOut.normalValue: No abnormality on the repeat study

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Fall in Glasgow Coma Scale, pupil inequality, limb weakness, increasing headache or persistent vomiting
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Minimum record: Glasgow Coma Scale, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.10).
ruleOut.normalValue: Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 with unchanged pupils, limb movements and vital signs for age

clinicalManagement.title: Triage and remote advice
actions: Send the child to a hospital emergency department if there was loss of consciousness, amnesia, persistent headache, vomiting, irritability or altered behaviour (especially under 5), safeguarding concern, or a bleeding or clotting disorder (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.2.3).
Use an emergency ambulance for impaired consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, suspected complex skull fracture or a high-energy injury (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.2.2).
Do not refer a child for a head scan directly from the community (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.3.19).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess in the emergency department
actions: Assess with the paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale and record its three components with the total (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.3.1 and 1.3.3).
Ask about mechanism, loss of consciousness, amnesia, vomiting, drowsiness and bleeding or clotting disorders; screen for non-accidental injury (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10 and 1.5.11).
Manage pain effectively because pain can raise intracranial pressure (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.3.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide about the head scan
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 hour of risk factor identified
actions: Scan within 1 hour for any single factor in Recommendation 1.5.10 (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Scan within 1 hour if more than 1 factor in Recommendation 1.5.11 is present (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).
Use the PECARN low-risk features as additional reassurance when deciding not to scan, not as a replacement for the NICE criteria (PECARN rule study, Section Findings).
Minimise radiation dose while keeping image quality (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.7).

clinicalManagement.title: Observe if only one factor is present
actions: Observe for at least 4 hours from the time of injury if only one factor from Recommendation 1.5.11 is present (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.12).
Chart half-hourly for 2 hours, then hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.11).
Scan within 1 hour if Glasgow Coma Scale falls below 15, vomiting recurs or drowsiness recurs (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.12).
Observe babies and children under 5 only in units with experienced staff (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.17).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate deterioration
actions: Reassess urgently for agitation, a sustained 1-point Glasgow Coma Scale fall for 30 minutes, severe or increasing headache, persistent vomiting, or new neurological signs (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.13).
Have a second competent observer confirm deterioration, but do not delay calling the doctor if none is free (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.14).
Consider an immediate scan once deterioration is confirmed (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.15).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge safely
actions: Discharge only when the Glasgow Coma Scale is 15, or consciousness is normal on the paediatric scale in preverbal children, and a competent adult can supervise at home (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.10.4 and 1.10.5).
Give verbal and printed age-appropriate advice, including the return signs and that an adult should stay with the child for the first 24 hours (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.10.8 and 1.10.9).
Write to the general practitioner within 48 hours and copy the health visitor or school nurse (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.10.12).

regimens.indication: Headache or pain after a minor head injury in a child assessed as safe for home
regimens.patientGroup: Children aged 2 to 11 years (use weight where known)
regimens.genericName: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) oral suspension 160 mg per 5 mL
regimens.dose: Dose by weight band, or by age if weight is unknown: 24 to 35 lb (2 to 3 years) 5 mL; 36 to 47 lb (4 to 5 years) 7.5 mL; 48 to 59 lb (6 to 8 years) 10 mL; 60 to 71 lb (9 to 10 years) 12.5 mL; 72 to 95 lb (11 years) 15 mL (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions). Under 24 lb or under 2 years: ask a doctor. Dilution and preparation: none; shake well before use and measure with the supplied dosing cup (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions).
regimens.frequency: Repeat every 4 hours while symptoms last; no more than 5 doses in 24 hours (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions)
regimens.duration: Short course while symptoms last; stop and ask a doctor if pain gets worse or lasts more than 5 days (Children's acetaminophen label, Stop use and ask a doctor)
adjustments: Under 2 years or under 24 lb: a doctor sets the dose (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions).
Liver disease: ask a doctor before use (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
Do not give with any other medicine containing acetaminophen (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
Ask a doctor or pharmacist if the child takes warfarin (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Worsening or increasing headache, repeated vomiting or drowsiness: return at once rather than increase the dose (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.13).
Total acetaminophen given in 24 hours (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions).
Skin reaction: stop and seek help (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
contraindications: Allergy to acetaminophen or any inactive ingredient (Children's acetaminophen label, Do not use).
More than 5 doses in 24 hours (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).

branches.label: Headache or pain after a head injury in a child assessed as safe for home
branches.entryCriteria: Child aged 2 years or older with a headache or pain after a minor head injury who has been assessed, does not meet scan criteria or has a normal scan, and has a competent adult at home; under 2 years only on a doctor's instruction.

medicationPlan.note: Most children need no medicine. Plain paracetamol (acetaminophen) is written for headache or pain once a child has been assessed and cleared for home, because untreated pain can raise intracranial pressure (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.3.11) and the label is the only paediatric dosing source read. The dose is taken from a United States children's label. Do not give pain relief to mask a worsening headache; a severe or increasing headache is a trigger to return (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.13). SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Scan within 1 hour: single risk factor
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Suspected non-accidental injury; seizure; Glasgow Coma Scale below 14 (below 15 if under 1 year); below 15 at 2 hours; suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture or tense fontanelle; focal deficit; baby under 1 year with head swelling over 5 cm (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.10).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Scan within 1 hour: more than one factor
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: More than 1 of: loss of consciousness over 5 minutes, abnormal drowsiness, 3 or more vomits, dangerous mechanism, amnesia over 5 minutes, bleeding or clotting disorder (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.11).

Only 1 factor from the group above: observe for at least 4 hours from injury and scan within 1 hour if Glasgow Coma Scale falls below 15, vomiting recurs or drowsiness recurs (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.5.12).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: PECARN low risk, age under 2 years
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Normal mental status, no scalp haematoma except frontal, no loss of consciousness or under 5 seconds, non-severe mechanism, no palpable skull fracture, acting normally per parent: negative predictive value 100% (PECARN rule study, Section Findings).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: PECARN low risk, age 2 years and over
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Normal mental status, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, non-severe mechanism, no basilar skull fracture signs, no severe headache: negative predictive value 99.95% (PECARN rule study, Section Findings).
Half-hourly for 2 hours, hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly; return to half-hourly if the child deteriorates (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.9.11 and 1.9.12).

guidelineComparison.title: Who needs a head scan, observation or discharge

values: Any one: non-accidental injury, seizure, Glasgow Coma Scale below 14, skull fracture signs, focal deficit; or more than one moderate-risk factor
Only one moderate-risk factor: loss of consciousness over 5 minutes, drowsiness, 3 or more vomits, dangerous mechanism, amnesia over 5 minutes, bleeding disorder
No risk factor, recovered, Glasgow Coma Scale of 15
Computed tomography head scan, resuscitate and involve neurosurgery per findings
Chart observations; scan if Glasgow Coma Scale falls, vomiting recurs or drowsiness recurs
Written advice and a responsible adult at home for 24 hours

guidelineComparison.note: NICE NG232, Section Recommendations 1.5 and 1.10; PECARN rule study, Section Findings.

teaching.scope: Emergency, urgent care and primary health centre doctors and nurses in Saudi Arabia assessing a child under 16 years with a head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13 to 15: decide who needs a computed tomography (CT) head scan within 1 hour, who needs at least 4 hours of observation, who can go home, and what to tell the family. Uses NICE NG232 (2023), the PECARN rule study and Saudi paediatric data. Not for children with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12 or less, penetrating injury or major trauma (follow the paediatric trauma pathway).
learningObjectives: Scan within 1 hour for any single high-risk factor or more than one moderate factor.
With only one moderate factor, observe for at least 4 hours before deciding.
Use the paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale and record its parts.
Always screen for non-accidental injury in a baby or child.
pitfalls: Missing a seizure or vomiting history in the story.
Not using the grimace score in preverbal children.
Discharging before a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15.
keyPoints: Do not scan from the community.
Do not discharge a child with no competent adult at home.
A normal examination does not remove the need for return advice.

patientEducation: Most children who bump their head are fine, but watch them closely.
An adult should stay with your child for the first 24 hours.

Come back at once if your child vomits again, becomes very sleepy or hard to wake, has a seizure, a worsening headache, weakness, clear fluid from the nose or ear, or seems confused or very irritable.
Give paracetamol for pain as the label says; it is not a reason to delay coming back if symptoms get worse.
Some children seem better then have problems later, so keep the written advice and the contact number.
lifestyleAndDiet: Rest for the first day and return to nursery or school and sport gradually as recovery allows.
Use helmets, seat belts and child seats; supervise babies on changing tables and stairs.
Report any worry that the injury was not an accident to a doctor or nurse.
mdtReferrals: Emergency doctor and nurse; paediatrician; radiologist and radiographer; neurosurgeon on call; safeguarding team; general practitioner, health visitor or school nurse.
dischargeCriteria: Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 (or normal consciousness on the paediatric scale); no scan criteria or a normal scan; competent adult at home for 24 hours; verbal and printed advice given; general practitioner letter within 48 hours.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Return at once for deterioration; review of persistent symptoms by the general practitioner or paediatric team; general practitioner letter within 48 hours of discharge (NICE NG232, Recommendation 1.10.12).
